newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Conservatives gaining on ruling Liberals.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Conservatives gaining on ruling Liberals.

text.p: Canada's Conservatives have gained on the ruling Liberals, who nonetheless maintain a crushing lead ahead of elections expected next year, a poll released on Monday showed.

The Angus Reid poll, commissioned by the Southam newspapers, showed the Liberals with 47 percent support in November -- their lowest since the October 1993, election. It was also a fall from 52 percent in October and from a peak of 63 percent in February, 1995.

The Conservatives, which were reduced in 1993 from a governing majority in the House of Commons to only two out of 295 seats, have risen to 18 percent support, up from 13 percent in October and five percent in February, 1994.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien was expected to call elections in 1997, possibly as early as the spring.

Conservative leader Jean Charest has been actively trying to rebuild support but was unable to rely on as large a team as his nearest rival, Preston Manning of the populist Reform Party, which has 51 members of Parliament.

But the Angus Reid poll said Manning's message of tax cuts and family values did not seem to have caught on across the country. Reform, which won 19 percent of the votes in 1993, slipped in November to 11 percent from 14 percent in October.

Part of the movement may have come from the change in methodology Angus Reid has used since September when it started pressing the undecided to show which party they would lean toward. Reform's limited support tends to be firmer than the Conservatives' and would not likely gain from this change.
Chretien's Liberals, which have moved to the right fiscally since the election, were banking on Reformers and Conservatives splitting what remained of the right-wing vote.

But the socialist New Democratic Party was beginning to emerge as a threat on their left flank. It won only seven percent of the vote in 1993 but has edged up to 11 percent in the poll, tied with Reform.
The survey of 1,520 Canadians was conducted on Nov. 26 to Dec. 2. Results were expected to carry a 2.5 percentage point margin of error 19 times out of 20.
